title: Feelings in depth
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: A feeling hangs off the verb with bi-: ashʿuru bi-at-taʿab, word for word "I feel with the tiredness". The bi- is not optional and it is not new — it is L1-M2's clitic doing a fresh job. What IS new is that the feeling is a NOUN (taʿab, farḥ, qalaq, khawf) where English reaches for an adjective.

yuʿjibunī is Arabic's backwards verb, and it is the shape to take away from this module: the thing you like is the SUBJECT and you are the object. yuʿjibunī hādhā al-kitāb is "this book pleases me". So the verb agrees with the THING — yuʿjibunī for a masculine one, tuʿjibunī for a feminine one — and never with you. Spanish me gusta, Italian mi piace and Marathi मला आवडतो are the same machine; English is the odd one out.

Arabic also keeps a feeling as a POSSESSION: ʿindī khawf ("I have a fear"), ladayya qalaq ("I have an anxiety"). That is L1-M7's ʿindī doing for a state what it did for a key or a car. ladayya is its more careful twin and means the same thing here.

A feeling adjective AGREES with whoever feels it — saʿīd / saʿīda, ḥazīn / ḥazīna, qaliq / qaliqa, mutaḥammis / mutaḥammisa, mutaʾakkid / mutaʾakkida. English adjectives never move for anybody, so the feminine -a is the habit to build. saʿīda, ḥazīna and taʿbāna were already yours from L1: this module only puts them to work.

lastu is "I am not" — the first-person cell of L2-M7's laysa. The adjective after it goes ACCUSATIVE and shows it: lastu mutaʾakkidan, lastu ḥazīnan, lastu saʿīdan. Nothing else in the sentence changes, and that -an is the only case ending written on this ladder.

words.note: To feel. It takes bi- before the feeling, always: ashʿuru bi-at-taʿab. tashʿuru is you or she, yashʿuru is he.
Tiredness, the NOUN behind L1-M5's adjective taʿbān. t is a sun letter, so the article assimilates: bi-at-taʿab, never bi-al-taʿab.

sentences.trap: English says "I feel tired" with an adjective and nothing in between. Arabic says "I feel with the tiredness" — a preposition and a noun. Drop the bi- and the sentence stops making sense.
sentences.sound: ash-ʿU-ru bit-ta-ʿAB — the bi- leans onto the noun and is never said on its own.

variations.cue: I feel tired in the evening
variations.changed: when: al-yawm → fī al-masāʾ, L1-M4's evening

variations.cue: You feel tired
variations.changed: who feels: ashʿuru → tashʿuru

mistake.why: The English shape carried over whole. taʿbān is the adjective from L1-M5 and it cannot follow ashʿuru: the verb wants bi- and a noun — ashʿuru bi-at-taʿab. anā taʿbān on its own is fine, and is the shorter way to say it.

sentences.usage: The everyday answer to kayfa ḥāluka on a long day, and the frame the rest of this module hangs on.
sentences.mnemonic: You do not feel tired. You feel WITH the tiredness.

sentences.cue: I feel anxious before the exam

words.note: Anxiety, the noun. q is a moon letter, so the article stays al-: bi-al-qalaq. Its adjective qaliq is one vowel away and is a different word — see S08.

sentences.trap: qalaq (the feeling) and qaliq (the person) are one spelling in Arabic script and two words in speech. Which one you want decides whether you need bi- or nothing at all.
sentences.sound: QA-laq, both vowels short and flat — not qa-LAAQ.

variations.cue: I feel anxious before the meeting
variations.changed: before what: al-imtiḥān → al-ijtimāʿ

variations.cue: He feels anxious today
variations.changed: who feels: ashʿuru → yashʿuru

mistake.why: qaliq is "anxious", the adjective for a person. After bi- you need the feeling itself: bi-al-qalaq.

sentences.usage: Said before anything with a result attached — an exam, an interview, a hospital appointment.
sentences.mnemonic: qalaq is the weather; qaliq is the person standing in it.

words.cue: it pleases me, I like it
words.note: Pleases me. The thing liked is the subject, so the verb follows IT: yuʿjibunī for a masculine thing, tuʿjibunī for a feminine one. The -nī on the end is you.

sentences.trap: English puts the liker first and the liked thing second. Arabic does the reverse, and the verb agrees with what an English speaker thinks is the wrong end. If you have met Spanish gusta or Marathi आवडतो you already own this shape.
sentences.sound: yuʿ-ji-BU-nee — the ʿ is the throat catch from L1's ʿindī, not a plain a.

variations.cue: I like this restaurant
variations.changed: what pleases: al-kitāb → al-maṭʿam

variations.cue: I like the work at this company
variations.changed: what pleases: a thing → an activity, L3-M2's al-ʿamal

mistake.why: This is English word order forced onto the Arabic verb, and it says roughly "I please this book". The book does the pleasing: yuʿjibunī hādhā al-kitāb.

sentences.usage: The polite, unexcited way to approve of something — a book, a film, a flat, a job.
sentences.mnemonic: The book pleases me. I never please the book.

words.note: S03's verb with the feminine subject prefix: al-mūsīqā is feminine, so it is tuʿjibunī. Nothing about you changed — the t- is the thing, not you.

sentences.trap: The t- here is not "you". It is the feminine of the THING. A learner who reads tuʿjibunī as "you please me" has the sentence inside out.
sentences.sound: tuʿ-ji-BU-nee — same shape as S03, one letter forward.

variations.cue: I like coffee
variations.changed: what pleases: al-mūsīqā → al-qahwa, also feminine

variations.cue: I really like Arabic
variations.changed: what pleases: the music → the language itself

mistake.why: al-mūsīqā is feminine, so the verb has to be tuʿjibunī. This is the one agreement the backwards verb still asks of you, and it looks at the thing, never at you.

sentences.usage: Taste, stated plainly — the sentence that follows "what do you listen to?".
sentences.mnemonic: Feminine thing, feminine verb — and you are still just -nī.

sentences.cue: I have a fear of exams

words.note: Fear, as a thing you have. What you fear comes in with min: khawf min al-imtiḥānāt. L1-M7's ʿindī holds it exactly as it held a key.

sentences.trap: English turns fear into an adjective — "I am afraid". In Arabic an adjective of fear describes your CHARACTER, not your Tuesday. ʿindī khawf keeps it a state, which is what you meant.
sentences.sound: KHAWF, one syllable, the kh scraped at the back like Scottish loch.

variations.cue: I have a fear of the exam
variations.changed: one exam instead of exams

variations.cue: You have a fear of exams
variations.changed: who has it: ʿindī → ʿindaka

mistake.why: That is "I am fear". A feeling noun needs a holder: ʿindī khawf, or ladayya khawf.

sentences.usage: How a state gets said without claiming it is who you are — useful with a doctor, a teacher or a friend.
sentences.mnemonic: You do not BE fear. You HAVE it, and you can put it down.

sentences.cue: I have anxiety because of work

words.note: The careful twin of L1-M7's ʿindī. Same meaning, higher register — what a doctor or a form would use. Either is correct here.

sentences.trap: ladayya and ʿindī are not two grammars, only two registers. Choosing between them is a matter of who you are talking to, never of what you mean.
sentences.sound: la-DAY-ya — the doubled y is held, la-DAY-yaa.

variations.cue: I have anxiety because of the appointment
variations.changed: the cause: al-ʿamal → al-mawʿid

variations.cue: I have anxiety because of work
variations.changed: register: ladayya → the everyday ʿindī

mistake.why: You cannot HAVE an adjective. What ladayya holds is the noun: ladayya qalaq. anā qaliq is the adjective sentence, and it needs no ladayya at all.

sentences.usage: The register you would use at a counter, in a clinic, or in anything written down.
sentences.mnemonic: ʿindī for a friend, ladayya for a form.

words.note: Excited. An ordinary adjective: mutaḥammisa for a woman, mutaḥammisūn for a group. Same mu- shape as L1-M7's mashghūl family.

sentences.trap: This one really is an adjective, so no bi- and no ʿindī. The module's three shapes are not interchangeable: noun feelings take a holder, adjectives take agreement.
sentences.sound: mu-ta-ḤAM-mis — the ḥ is the breathy one from L1's alḥamdu lillāh.

variations.cue: She is very excited
variations.changed: who: anā → hiya, and the adjective takes -a

variations.cue: The staff are excited today
variations.changed: who: one person → a group, and the adjective takes -ūn

mistake.why: ʿindī holds nouns. mutaḥammis is an adjective and simply follows anā: anā mutaḥammis.

sentences.usage: Before a trip, a first day, a wedding — the everyday positive that is not just saʿīd.

sentences.cue: She is anxious but I am happy

words.note: Anxious, the adjective — one vowel from S02's noun qalaq and the same letters in Arabic. Agrees: qaliqa for a woman, qaliqūn for a group.

sentences.trap: saʿīd and saʿīda have been yours since L1-M1, ḥazīn and ḥazīna since L1-M9. This module opens no new feminine for them: it puts an agreement you already own next to two adjectives that follow the same rule.
sentences.sound: QA-li-qa — three light syllables, no stress at the end.

variations.cue: He is anxious today
variations.changed: who: hiya → huwa, and the -a goes

variations.cue: She is anxious but she is happy
variations.changed: both halves feminine, so both adjectives take -a

mistake.why: Both agreements are backwards: hiya needs qaliqa, and a male speaker needs saʿīd. The adjective looks at who it describes, and it looks every single time.

sentences.usage: The sentence that holds two people's moods in one breath — and the one that catches a missing agreement fastest.
sentences.mnemonic: Two people, two endings, one lākin between them.

sentences.cue: I am not sure about the appointment

words.note: The "I" cell of L2-M7's laysa. It negates a whole adjective sentence on its own — no lā, and no separate anā needed.
Sure. After lastu it goes accusative and shows -an: mutaʾakkidan. The ʾ is a hamza, a catch in the throat, not the ʿ of ʿindī.

sentences.trap: English negates with an extra word and leaves the adjective alone. Arabic changes the verb AND the adjective's ending — one word does the negating, and the -an is the receipt.
sentences.sound: LAS-tu mu-ta-ʾAK-ki-dan — the hamza in the middle is a tiny stop, like the catch in "uh-oh".

variations.cue: I am not sure about the number
variations.changed: about what: al-mawʿid → ar-raqm

variations.cue: I am not happy today
variations.changed: which adjective — and it takes the same -an

mistake.why: lā negates verbs, not adjective sentences. For "I am not" plus an adjective the word is lastu, and the adjective picks up -an: lastu mutaʾakkidan.

sentences.usage: The honest hedge at a counter or on the phone, and the softest way to say no to a plan.

sentences.cue: I am not sad — I feel joy

words.note: The accusative of L1-M9's ḥazīn — the shape it takes after lastu, and its first appearance on this ladder. Tap ḥazīn for the plain word.
Joy, the noun. f is a moon letter, so the article stays al-: bi-al-farḥ. The bigger, warmer word next to saʿīd.
The accusative of L1-M1's saʿīd, used after lastu — see this sentence's second variation. Tap saʿīd for the plain word.

sentences.trap: Two grammars in one breath: lastu takes the accusative adjective, ashʿuru takes bi- and a noun. Neither borrows the other's shape, and mixing them is this module's commonest slip.
sentences.sound: LAS-tu ḥa-ZEE-nan — a real pause at the comma, then ash-ʿU-ru bil-FARḤ.

variations.cue: I am not sad today
variations.changed: the second half dropped, the -an kept

variations.cue: I am not happy — I feel anxious
variations.changed: both feelings flipped, both frames held

mistake.why: Two halves, two errors: the adjective after lastu needs -an, and the noun after ashʿuru needs bi-. lastu ḥazīnan, ashʿuru bi-al-farḥ.

sentences.usage: The correction you make when someone reads your quiet face wrong — and the module's whole grammar in five words.
sentences.mnemonic: -an after lastu, bi- after ashʿuru. Two doors, two keys.

comprehensionPool.cue: I feel anxious before the exam
I have a fear of exams
I have anxiety because of work
She is anxious but I am happy
I am not sure about the appointment
I am not sad — I feel joy
I like the work at this company
